title: Three job classes in four years, with pay up by half or more
question: Who moved through three or more job classes within four fiscal years while their regular salary rose by at least half, and in which departments?
finding: Of 20,023 employees who can be followed by name across a four-year window, 291 (1.5%) held three or more classes in it with regular salary up by half or more; 85 of them started in a trainee, apprentice, aide or junior class. For comparison, the middle rise over four years for people who stayed in one class was 14.9%. Of the other 206, 89 ended in an exempt appointment and 5 in a class with one or two holders. Among departments with 100 or more followed employees the rate is highest in Homelessness Services (6.2%), Port (5.5%), Emergency Management (4.0%).
how: City payroll file, fiscal 2017 to 2026. Only names that pass the matching rules are followed (one spelling, one person, rare): 48,514 of 71,958. For each window of four fiscal years in which the person’s main job has 1,800 paid hours or more in the first and last year, the main job classes are listed and regular salary in the last year is compared with the first; overtime and other pay are left out. Listed: three or more different classes and a salary at least 1.5 times the starting one; the window with the largest rise is kept for each person. People who did not start in a trainee-type class come first, by the size of the rise in dollars.
limits: General raises and step increases lift pay even for people who stay put, as the comparison figure shows. Many of these paths are a class series climbed one step a year, or a move from the bargaining-unit classes into management after an examination; in the uniformed services a move from a rank to a chief’s post is by appointment. A rare name can still be two people. The payroll cannot show whether each step was by examination, by exempt appointment or by reclassifying the post around the person; the appointment forms for each step would.
